verdict.rationale: AWS documents IAM OIDC identity providers that connect CI systems such as GitHub Actions to AWS, and role assumption that issues temporary session credentials with no long-term access keys, so the core of the story is first-party. The evidence covers only fragments, though: there is no end-to-end setup walkthrough, nothing on services' own workload identity, and nothing on preventing long-lived keys from being issued. missing for 10: end-to-end documented OIDC-to-role setup flow, workload identity for non-CI services/compute, controls that block or detect long-lived access keys, credential lifetime/scoping details, independent or hands-on corroboration.

support.subject: As a security engineer, nothing ships a long-lived key — OIDC/workload identity federation issues short-lived credentials to CI and services, documented end to end

citations.quote: OIDC connects applications, like GitHub Actions, that do not run on AWS to AWS resources.
when you assume a role, it provides you with temporary security credentials for your role session.
a role does not have standard long-term credentials such as a password or access keys associated with it.
With an identity provider (IdP), you can manage your user identities outside of AWS and give these external user identities permissions to use AWS resources in your account.
